title: Supply and demand: shifts and new equilibria
summary: You know the two curves. Check that you can tell a shift from a slide and predict what happens to price and quantity.
objective: Given a market event, say which curve shifts and which way, then predict the new price and quantity, even when both curves move.

hook.prompt: A frost wipes out a third of a big coffee harvest, and coffee prices jump. A news anchor says: "Higher prices will cut demand, which will bring prices back down." Is the anchor right?

options.text: Yes: that's how markets correct themselves
options.feedback: It sounds right, but it mixes up two different things that both get called "demand".

options.text: No: higher prices cut the amount people buy, but that doesn't push prices back down
No: scarcity makes demand rise, so prices climb further
options.feedback: Scarcity here is on the supply side. Buyers' wants didn't change because of the frost.

hook.explanation: People buy less coffee at the higher price, but that's a response to the price, not a new cause pushing it down. The first concept shows why.

bricks.title: Slide along, or shift the curve?
bricks.body: Only a change in the good's **own price** moves you *along* a curve: a change in **quantity demanded** or **quantity supplied**. Everything else **shifts** the whole curve. Demand shifts with income, tastes, expectations, and the prices of substitutes or complements. Supply shifts with input costs, technology, and the number of sellers. *Example:* coffee beans get dearer, so cafés' costs rise and latte **supply** shifts left. Pricier lattes then cut quantity demanded; demand itself hasn't moved.

visual.alt: Two small graphs. Left: a point slides down one demand curve. Right: the whole demand curve moves right to a new position.

bricks.prompt: Bus fares rise. Complete the analyst's notes.
bricks.template: Fewer people ride the bus: a fall in the [[a]] of bus rides. More people buy bikes instead: a rise in the [[b]] for bikes.

mistakes.feedback: The bus's own fare changed, so riders slide along the bus demand curve; the curve itself stays put.
Riders are buyers, and the bus company didn't change what it offers. This is about the demand side.
Bike prices didn't change. A substitute's price did, and that shifts the whole bike demand curve.
Bike makers' costs and technology didn't change. It's buyers who want more bikes at every price.

bricks.explanation: Bus riders respond to the bus's own price: a slide along. Bikes are a substitute, so pricier buses shift bike demand right.

bricks.prompt: A ride-share app raises fares at rush hour, and more drivers log on. How would an economist describe the extra drivers?

options.text: A rise in the quantity supplied of rides
A rise in the supply of rides
options.feedback: Drivers are reacting to the fare, which is the ride's own price. That's a slide along the supply curve, not a shift.

options.text: A rise in the demand for rides
options.feedback: Drivers are sellers, so they sit on the supply side. Riders' wants are a different curve.

options.text: A fall in the demand for rides, since riders pay more
options.feedback: Riders taking fewer rides at a higher fare is a fall in quantity demanded, and the question asks about drivers.

bricks.explanation: The fare is the ride's own price. Drivers offering more rides at a higher fare is a slide up the existing supply curve.

bricks.prompt: The price of home printers falls sharply. What happens in the market for ink cartridges?

options.text: Demand for ink shifts right
Quantity demanded of ink rises along its curve
options.feedback: A slide along needs a change in ink's own price. Printers are another good, so their price shifts the ink curve.

options.text: Supply of ink shifts right
options.feedback: Ink makers' costs, technology, and numbers didn't change. The change comes from buyers.

options.text: Demand for ink shifts left
options.feedback: That's the pattern for substitutes. Printers and ink are used together, so they're complements.

bricks.hint: Are printers and ink substitutes or complements?
bricks.explanation: Printers and ink are complements. Cheaper printers mean more printers in homes, so people want more ink at every ink price.

bricks.prompt: Each event hits the market for strawberries. Sort them by what happens in that market.

items.text: A widely shared study says strawberries boost memory
The price of whipped cream falls
Shoppers expect strawberries to be cheaper next week
A new variety yields twice as many berries per plant
Several new farms start growing strawberries
Strawberries go on sale and shoppers buy more
Growers pick more of the crop as the strawberry price climbs

bricks.hint: First ask: is this strawberries' own price changing, or something else?
bricks.explanation: Tastes, a complement's price, and expectations shift demand. Wages, yields, and new farms shift supply. Only strawberries' own price causes a slide along.

bricks.prompt: A colleague wrote these notes on the e-scooter market. Tap the line that gets it wrong.

visual.html:
E-scooter market: this quarter

Draft notes

  • Battery prices fell → scooter supply shifts right
  • City bans scooters on sidewalks → scooter demand shifts left
  • Scooter prices fell → scooter demand shifts right
  • Bike-share fees doubled → scooter demand shifts right

bricks.hint: Which line is about the scooter's own price?
bricks.explanation: Cheaper scooters mean people buy more along the same demand curve: a rise in quantity demanded. The other lines name real shifters: input costs, rules, a substitute's price.

bricks.title: Three steps to the new equilibrium
bricks.body: To predict where a market lands, run three steps. **1.** Which curve shifts? **2.** Which way? **3.** Read the result off the table. *Example:* a heatwave shifts demand for fans right, so their price and quantity both rise. When **both** curves shift at once, take each shift alone. Where they push a variable the same way, you're sure of it; where they clash, it's ambiguous until you know which shift is bigger.

visual.alt: Table: demand right raises price and quantity; demand left lowers both; supply right lowers price, raises quantity; supply left raises price, lowers quantity.

bricks.prompt: Finish the three steps for this case.
bricks.template: A big study finds oat milk is healthier than people thought. Demand for oat milk shifts [[dir]], so its price [[p]] and the quantity sold [[q]].

mistakes.feedback: Better health news makes people want more oat milk at every price, which is a shift to the right.
A falling price comes from demand shifting left or supply shifting right. Neither happened here.
Sellers offer more at the higher price, so the quantity traded goes up, not down.
Only one curve moved, so nothing offsets it. Demand shifting right raises both price and quantity.

bricks.explanation: Tastes moved toward oat milk, so demand shifts right. Demand right means price up and quantity up.

bricks.prompt: A new machine halves the cost of making solar panels. What happens to the price and quantity of panels sold?

options.text: Price falls, quantity rises
Price rises, quantity falls
options.feedback: That's supply shifting left. Lower costs let makers offer more at every price: a shift right.

options.text: Price falls, quantity falls
options.feedback: That's demand shifting left. Buyers' wants didn't change; makers' costs did.

options.text: Price falls, quantity unchanged, since demand didn't move
options.feedback: Demand didn't shift, but cheaper panels raise the quantity demanded along it, so more panels are sold.

bricks.explanation: Lower costs shift supply right. Supply right means a lower price and, as buyers slide down their demand curve, a larger quantity.

bricks.prompt: Over one year, concert ticket prices rose while fewer tickets were sold. Which single shift fits both facts?

options.text: Supply shifted left
Demand shifted right
options.feedback: Demand right raises price, but it raises quantity too. Here quantity fell.

options.text: Demand shifted left
options.feedback: Demand left lowers quantity, but it lowers price too. Here price rose.

options.text: Supply shifted right
options.feedback: Supply right does the opposite of what happened: price down, quantity up.

bricks.hint: Price and quantity moved in opposite directions. Which curve does that when it shifts?
bricks.explanation: Demand shifts move price and quantity together; supply shifts move them apart. Price up with quantity down means supply shifted left, for example fewer tour dates.

bricks.prompt: Cheaper fertiliser boosts the corn harvest. In the same season, ethanol plants start buying much more corn. What can you predict for sure about the corn market?

options.text: Quantity rises; the price change is ambiguous
Price rises; the quantity change is ambiguous
options.feedback: Take each shift alone. Supply right lowers price while demand right raises it, so price is the one that clashes.

options.text: Price falls and quantity rises
options.feedback: That's true only if the supply shift is bigger than the demand shift, and you don't know that.

options.text: Both price and quantity are ambiguous
options.feedback: Both shifts push quantity up, so quantity isn't in doubt. Only price clashes.

bricks.hint: Write down what each shift does to price and to quantity, then compare.
bricks.explanation: Supply right: price down, quantity up. Demand right: price up, quantity up. Quantity rises for sure; price depends on which shift is bigger.

challenge.prompt: A frost destroys much of the orange crop. Nothing happens to apples. What happens in the market for apple juice?

options.text: Apple juice price and quantity both rise
Apple juice price rises and quantity falls
options.feedback: That's a supply shift left, but the frost hit oranges, not apple juice makers' costs. Apple juice changes through its buyers.

options.text: Nothing changes; the frost is in another market
options.feedback: The frost makes orange juice dearer, and apple juice is a substitute, so it reaches the apple juice market through demand.

options.text: Quantity demanded of apple juice rises along its curve; its price stays the same
options.feedback: Apple juice's own price didn't start this. A substitute's price did, which shifts the whole demand curve right and raises the price.

challenge.hint: Start in the orange market, then ask how apple juice is related to orange juice.
challenge.explanation:
Orange supply shifts left, so orange juice gets dearer.
Apple juice is a substitute, so its demand shifts right.
Demand right: price up, quantity up.

takeaways: Before calling it a shift, check whether the good's own price changed: if so, it's a slide along the curve.
Demand shifts with buyers' world (income, tastes, related prices, expectations); supply shifts with sellers' world (costs, technology, number of sellers).
Demand shifts move price and quantity together; supply shifts move them apart.
When both curves shift, take each alone: you can be sure of only the variable they push the same way.
